faqs.question: What does the CD34 Test – Haematology measure?
faqs.answer: The CD34 Test detect the presence of CD34 antigen on hematopoietic stem cells and precursor cells.

faqs.question: Why is the CD34 Test – Haematology done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose and monitor precursor leukaemia • To determine the extent, severity, and progression of the disease and assess treatment response • To guide treatment decisions, such as the need for stem cell transplantation • To evaluate the prognosis (outlook) for patients with precursor leukaemia

faqs.question: When is the CD34 Test – Haematology recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The CD34 Test – Haematology is recommended in the following situations: • When a patient shows symptoms suggestive of precursor leukaemia, such as unexplained fatigue, frequent infections, or easy bleeding/bruising • For those already diagnosed with precursor leukaemia to assess the stage and progression of the disease • To monitor treatment response and detect relapse in patients with precursor leukaemia • Before planning a stem cell transplantation for precursor leukaemia patients.

faqs.question: What if the results of the CD34 Test – Haematology are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal result may indicate precursor leukaemia.

faqs.question: What to expect during the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: During the CD34 Test – Haematology: • A small sample (3 ml) of your blood is collected using a needle. • The sample is sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: Before the CD34 Test – Haematology: • No specific preparations are required. • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking or medical conditions you have that may affect the test results. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the CD34 Test – Haematology include: • Complete blood count (CBC): To evaluate other blood cell counts and identify any abnormalities • Bone marrow biopsy: To obtain a sample of bone marrow for further analysis, if leukaemia is suspected. • Genetic testing: To assess specific genetic abnormalities associated with precursor leukaemia or guide treatment decisions.

faqs.question: What is the CD34 Test – Haematology also known as?
faqs.answer: CD34 immunophenotyping test, flow cytometry immunophenotyping for precursor leukaemia

faqs.question: What is precursor leukaemia?
faqs.answer: Precursor leukaemia, also known as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) or acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), is a type of blood cancer that affects immature blood cells, including stem cells. It is characterised by uncontrolled growth and accumulation of these abnormal cells in the bone marrow and bloodstream.
